catalog_locator: Phonology section (after Vowels), PDF page 14 of 22 (no printed page numbers in text layer)(lines 711-714
catalog_quote: Stress in Hobongan is irregular and unpredictable. There is a general preference to stress the first syllable of a bisyllabic word, but there are many exceptions. Hobongan does not appear to have syllable-weight stress, morae, or utterance-level rhythm patterns that would affect the stress patterns on any given word. Hobongan is not a tonal language. ... Hobongan does not have single-syllable consonant clusters phonemically, but /o/ in unstressed syllables is often reduced to the point of disappearing when it occurs before an approximant: /ko.la.ˈput/ (type of hard wood) → [kla.ˈput].

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated place in the publisher PDF we hold (p.14/22). The deciding source is a 2024 fieldwork sketch by the sole linguist working on the language; its stress paragraph is impressionistic but explicit (irregular/unpredictable, weak initial preference in disyllables, no weight sensitivity), and the classification 'lexical, non-strict, pervasive exceptions' follows it faithfully. No competing description exists: Glottolog has no grammar/phonology for hovo1239, Perkins's other papers are non-phonological, and Smith 2017 (downloaded now, first-hand Hovongan wordlist) makes no stress statement; its unexplained sporadic accent marks on varying syllables are at most consistent with non-fixed stress. Not 'well-sourced' because the source is a brief sketch without instrumental or distributional support; not 'at-risk' because nothing found contradicts it. One low-priority open item

sources.quote: No statement on Hovongan (or Müller-Schwaner) stress anywhere; every 'stress' hit concerns Merap, Segai-Modang, Hliboi Bidayuh, or W. Kalimantan Malayic. The Appendix 4 Hovongan wordlist (90 rows) carries sporadic, unexplained acute accents on 22 rows falling on varying syllables (e.g. kévaŋ, úsun, nísaŋ vs cokóm, katé, uvé, maŋá, cahálo); Smith's transcription conventions (sec. 1.5) do not define them, so they cannot be read as a stress analysis.
